Kitting out on a budget is a rite of passage, and finding the best gear for A2 and small bikes is mostly about spending wisely rather than spending big. When I passed my test the temptation was to blow the entire budget on the bike and ride away in a hoodie. Please do not do that. On a lighter machine like a Honda NC750X or a Kawasaki Z650 you are just as likely to have a low-speed spill in the wet as anyone, and the gear is the bit that decides whether you get up and dust yourself down or spend a fortnight off work. The good news is that value kit in 2026 is genuinely good, and you can be properly protected without remortgaging.

Where to spend and where to save

New riders always ask what to buy first. My honest order of priority is helmet, gloves, an armoured jacket, then protective jeans and boots. A helmet protects the one thing you cannot replace, and gloves save the hands you instinctively put out in a fall. Everything else is important, but that is the sequence I would follow if money were tight. Small bikes are cheap to run, which frees up a little more of the budget for kit than a thirsty litre bike would.

The helmet: safe does not mean expensive

You do not need to spend three figures plus to get a safe helmet. A HJC C10 Helmet is a proper full-face at an entry price, ECE 22.06 certified, and comfortable enough for a couple of hours in the saddle. The single most important thing is fit: a cheap helmet that fits your head shape is far safer than a pricey one that does not. Our best budget motorcycle helmets UK guide lists the standouts and explains what you actually gain as you spend more.

The best helmet is the one that fits, that you can afford, and that you will actually wear on every single ride, including the two-minute trip to the shop where most spills happen.

Protective jeans: the everyday hero

For a new rider on a small bike, a good pair of riding jeans is arguably the most useful garment you can own, because you will actually wear them. A pair of Roadskin Paranoid Kevlar Jeans looks like normal denim, takes CE knee and hip armour, and lines the impact zones with aramid fibre. You can ride to work, walk around all day, and ride home without changing. Our motorcycle riding jeans guide explains the difference between single-layer and lined constructions, which matters a lot for abrasion resistance.

The jacket and armour

A textile jacket is the natural first choice for a new rider: forgiving, weatherproof-ish, and armoured. A Weise Textile Jacket gives you CE armour at the shoulders and elbows and usually a pocket for a back protector, which I would add straight away. Check the fit with the armour sitting where it should over your joints, not halfway down your forearm.

Gloves for all seasons

Even in summer, wear gloves. A ventilated pair like the RST Urban Air Gloves keeps your hands cool and protected on a warm day around town, and they are cheap enough that a warmer winter pair later will not break the bank. Look for knuckle protection and a secure wrist closure so the glove cannot be flung off in a slide.

Layering and staying warm on a small bike

Small bikes offer less wind protection than a big faired tourer, so layering earns its keep. A decent Oxford Base Layer under your jacket traps warmth without bulk, and it wicks sweat on a warmer day too. British riding is all about managing changeable weather, and a good base layer plus a mid layer beats one enormous winter coat that is useless in June.

Waterproofs that live under the seat

You will get rained on. An Oxford Rainseal Oversuit is cheap, packs small, and pulls over everything when the clouds open on the A5 through Snowdonia. On a budget it is far better value than a premium laminated jacket you cannot afford yet, and it keeps your one good set of gear dry.

A sensible starter kit list

  • ECE 22.06 full-face helmet that fits your head shape.
  • Armoured textile jacket with a back protector added.
  • Kevlar-lined riding jeans with knee and hip armour.
  • Vented summer gloves now, warmer pair for winter later.
  • Packable waterproof oversuit and a base layer.
  • Over-ankle boots with a bit of protection, even budget touring boots.

Growing into your riding

The lovely thing about starting on a small bike is that the running costs leave room to build your kit gradually. A Honda CB500X or similar A2-friendly machine barely sips fuel, so a tank of petrol saved is a pair of gloves earned. When you are ready to venture further, our guide on how to tour on a small bike and our overview of A2 licence touring bikes will get you pointed at the right roads. Buy safe, buy for the weather, and upgrade as you go.
keyTakeaways: Kitting out well on a budget is about spending wisely, not spending big; 2026 value kit is genuinely good.
Priority order for new riders: helmet, gloves, armoured jacket, then protective jeans and boots.
A well-fitting entry helmet is safer than a pricey one that does not fit your head shape.
Riding jeans are the everyday hero because you will actually wear them every ride.
Layering and a packable oversuit beat one huge winter coat that is useless in June.

pros: Modern value kit protects properly without remortgaging.
Small bikes are cheap to run, freeing budget for gear.
You can build the kit gradually as running costs stay low.
cons: Tight budgets tempt new riders into dangerous under-dressing.
Cheaper gear may lack the refinement of premium kit.
Fit still needs checking carefully, especially on helmets.

faq.q: What gear should a new rider buy first?
faq.a: The honest order of priority is helmet, gloves, an armoured jacket, then protective jeans and boots. A helmet protects the one thing you cannot replace, and gloves save the hands you instinctively put out in a fall. Everything else matters, but that is the sequence to follow if money is tight. Small bikes are cheap to run, which frees up a little more budget for kit.

faq.q: Do I need an expensive helmet?
faq.a: No. You do not need to spend three figures to get a safe helmet. An entry-price full-face that is ECE 22.06 certified and comfortable for a couple of hours is plenty. The single most important thing is fit: a cheap helmet that fits your head shape is far safer than a pricey one that does not. Try several to find the shape that suits your head.

faq.q: Are riding jeans a good buy for a new rider?
faq.a: They are arguably the most useful garment you can own, because you will actually wear them. Good riding jeans look like normal denim, take CE knee and hip armour and line the impact zones with aramid fibre, so you can ride to work, walk around all day and ride home without changing. Look for single-layer construction for the best abrasion resistance.

faq.q: How do I stay warm and dry on a small bike on a budget?
faq.a: Small bikes offer less wind protection, so layering earns its keep. A decent base layer under your jacket traps warmth without bulk and wicks sweat on warmer days, so a base plus mid layer beats one enormous winter coat that is useless in June. Add a cheap packable oversuit that pulls over everything when the clouds open, which is far better value than a premium laminated jacket you cannot yet afford.

faq.q: What does a sensible starter kit list look like?
faq.a: An ECE 22.06 full-face helmet that fits your head shape, an armoured textile jacket with a back protector added, Kevlar-lined riding jeans with knee and hip armour, vented summer gloves now with a warmer pair later, a packable waterproof oversuit and a base layer, and over-ankle boots with some protection. That covers you safely for all-weather riding without overspending.
